description: 'Which should I learn?' guide for an English-speaking learner in the US. Written to inform, not to rank traditions. The evidence on what American congregations actually do is thin: one published survey measured one or two words. Every entry says so and tells the learner to check their own congregation.
evidenceNote: The only quantitative source read is Benor and Cohen's survey (BJPA). It asked which form of 'Festival of Booths' people use; 'soo-COAT' (Israeli) was chosen by 68% of Reform, 73% of Conservative, 70% of Modern Orthodox, 50% of Orthodox and 38% of Black Hat respondents, 'SUK-kiss' (Ashkenazic) by 34, 34, 47, 67 and 73% (people could pick both, so rows add to more than 100). Self-reported, snowball sample, not representative, one word. It tells you tendencies, not what your synagogue does.
universalAdvice: Ask the people you will pray with. Listen to a service or a recording from your own congregation before you choose.
Practice varies inside a single synagogue: the cantor, the rabbi, older members and the Torah reader may each say things differently.
Chabad.org's own article says all dialects of Hebrew are acceptable; it is a matter of community custom, not of right and wrong.

If you are unsure, learn the Israeli-based sounds first. They are what the Hebrew of Israel uses and what most non-Orthodox respondents in the survey reported, and the Ashkenazi switches (tav, kamatz, cholam, tsere, stress) can be added afterwards.

situations.title: A Reform synagogue in the US
situations.summary: Most likely Israeli-based sounds, which the app calls the American-synagogue setting. Expect some Ashkenazi forms in familiar words and songs.
caveats: In the survey, Reform respondents were the group most likely to choose the Israeli form of the one word asked about, but about a third also use the Ashkenazic form.
Individual cantors and older members often keep Ashkenazi habits.
situations.askFirst: Which pronunciation do the cantor and the Torah readers use, and is there a recording I can practise with?

situations.title: A Conservative synagogue in the US
situations.summary: Again, Israeli-based sounds are the more common choice in the survey, with a large Ashkenazic minority. Congregations differ.
caveats: One word measured: 73% chose the Israeli form, 34% the Ashkenazic form.
Congregations differ, and the survey cannot tell you which kind yours is.
situations.askFirst: Does the shul use Israeli-style pronunciation for Torah reading and for the siddur, or does it differ between the two?

situations.title: A Modern Orthodox synagogue in the US
situations.summary: Mixed. The survey found both forms common (70% Israeli, 47% Ashkenazic for the one word). Listen first.
caveats: Many Modern Orthodox people switch between forms depending on setting.
Torah reading and prayer may use a different pronunciation from everyday Hebrew words.
situations.askFirst: What do the rabbi and the baal koreh (Torah reader) use?

situations.title: An Orthodox or Haredi synagogue in the US
situations.summary: Ashkenazi pronunciation is more common here than elsewhere in the survey, but not universal. Half of the Orthodox respondents also reported the Israeli form, so Israeli-style and Sephardi communities exist inside Orthodoxy too.
caveats: Survey: 67% (Orthodox) and 73% (Black Hat) chose the Ashkenazic form of the one word, yet 50% and 38% chose the Israeli form.
Ashkenazi has regional dialects. ALEF models one common siddur style; your community's may differ (for example oy or ey for cholam).
situations.askFirst: Which dialect of Ashkenazi does my community use, and who can I copy?

situations.title: A Sephardi, Mizrahi or other non-Ashkenazi community
situations.summary: The app's Sephardi-values setting matches the vowels (a, e, i, o, u) but not your community's consonants, which may include pharyngeal het and ayin.
caveats: 'Sephardi' covers many communities with different habits (Spanish-Portuguese, North African, Balkan, Levantine, Iraqi, Yemenite and more).
ALEF does not model any of them in detail. Use it for reading practice and take the sounds from a member of your community.
situations.askFirst: Can someone from my community record or sit with me for the throat sounds and for how they say the prayers?

situations.title: Preparing to read Torah or lead prayers (for example for a bar or bat mitzvah)
situations.summary: Use the tradition your synagogue and teacher use. That choice is made by your community, not by this app.
caveats: Cantillation (the trope melodies) is a separate topic not taught here.
Take the recording or the teacher's reading as the final authority for your congregation.
situations.askFirst: Which pronunciation and which melodies does my teacher expect?

situations.title: Travelling or living in Israel
situations.summary: Learn the Modern Israeli sounds. Everyday Israeli Hebrew has no pharyngeals for most speakers, a back-of-the-throat r, and mostly final stress.
caveats: Some older Mizrahi Israelis still use pharyngeal sounds, and Israeli synagogues keep Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Mizrahi and Yemenite customs side by side.
ALEF does not teach Tel Aviv slang or informal fast speech: no source for those was found.
situations.askFirst: Is it for travel talk (Israeli track) or for services in Israel (ask the synagogue)?
